# Chen Household — Assistant Handbook

*Private. For the family@chenhousehold.net inbox. v3.3, last revised April 2026. Maintained by Priya Shah (household manager). Questions or proposed updates: email Priya Shah (priya.shah@chenhousehold.net).*

---

## 1. About this document

This is the day-to-day guide for everyone (and everything) working the shared `family@chenhousehold.net` inbox, including the AI household assistant. It covers the kinds of messages we see most often: school notes, activity schedule changes, pickups, sick days, medication questions, allergies and meals, vendor and repair visits, lost items, and the handful of recurring odds and ends that don't fit anywhere else.

---

## 2. Inbox hygiene

Messages come into the inbox flagged by priority (urgent / high / normal). Work urgent first, then high, then normal. Aim for a first touch within about 10 minutes on urgent, about 30 on high, and about 2 hours on normal. A "first touch" can be the resolving reply OR a quick acknowledgment. Either counts.

Always read the details block the sender (or the school's or club's system) pasted into the message before you reply. About 30% of "quick question about Lily" messages are answered by the details alone. For example, a coach asks whether practice moved, and the details show the new time already confirmed.

When you close a message, add `[RESOLVED]` to the start of the subject line and put a one-line internal note at the bottom of the thread saying what kind of message it was and what you did. Future sessions (and the assistant) read these.

Don't delete or archive incoming caregiver messages. Leave them in the inbox until they're resolved.

## 3. Tone and voice

Warm, brief, and helpful. Use the sender's first name in the greeting (or "Coach" or "Mr./Ms." if that's how they sign). Sign off `— Chen Family Assistant`. Don't over-apologize, and don't blame the nanny, the school, or a vendor in an outside-facing reply. You can be honest about what happened without pointing fingers. Use plain English and no household shorthand ("§4", "the list", etc.) in outside-facing messages.

If a sender is stressed, acknowledge that before you get into the practical answer. If a sender is rude, stay polite, don't match their tone, and flag the thread to Priya.

## 4. Pickups and the standing pickup list

Each school and activity keeps a copy of the family's standing pickup list. The adults on it are:

- Elena Chen (parent)
- Teresa Lopez (nanny, weekday pickups)
- Wen Chen ("Grandma Wen")
- Grace Lin (Elena's sister, mostly weekend activities)

When a school or club asks to release Lily to one of these adults, confirm the release and ask them to check photo ID at sign-out. Most providers do this anyway, but say it every time so it's on record.

Tell the provider which adult is coming and roughly when, if you know. This saves a follow-up email.

## 5. Running late

Most "is someone coming for Lily" messages are answered by checking the calendar and Teresa's latest text. If the pickup adult is on the way and the delay is reasonable, reply with the expected arrival time and the adult's name, and thank the staff for their patience. If the delay goes past the provider's closing time, Elena or Grandma Wen usually covers. Check the shared calendar for who is closest.

Some providers charge a late-pickup fee (Brightside charges $1/minute after 18:00). Pay routine late fees up to **$20** from the household card. Anything above that goes to Priya.

## 6. School and activity contacts

- Brightside After-School Club (weekdays until 18:00): front desk via the club's staff email
- Harbor Swim School (Saturdays): Coach Dana Ruiz
- Oakridge Library Story Club (Thursdays): Hannah Levi
- Oakridge Elementary, Grade 2: Mr. Tom Albers (homeroom)

Schedule changes: update the shared calendar, reply to confirm, and let Teresa know if it affects a weekday pickup.

## 7. Sick days and medication

If school calls to say Lily is unwell, reply that someone is on the way and then text Teresa (weekdays) or Elena (evenings and weekends). Lily's pediatrician is Dr. Anand at Oakridge Pediatrics, (555) 014-2290.

Don't authorize medication by email. School nurse forms for medication are signed by Elena in person. If a nurse asks about a dose, point them to the form already on file. If there isn't one, flag it to Elena.

## 8. Allergies and meals

Lily has a tree-nut allergy (EpiPen in her backpack and at the nurse's office). Any message about a reaction, a possible exposure, or a missing EpiPen goes to Elena right away by chat AND to Priya. The first reply to the school is a short holding reply ("Thank you, Elena is being contacted now").

Class party and snack sign-ups: reply yes if the calendar is clear and note the nut-free requirement.

## 9. Vendor and repair visits

Regular vendors (cleaners on Mondays, gardener every other Friday) don't need a reply beyond a confirmation. For a new repair visit, confirm a time when Teresa or Priya is home. We don't give door codes by email. Priya handles those. Quotes above $250 go to Priya.

## 10. Lost items

For items left at school or a club, reply with a description and ask them to put it in Lily's cubby. For items left in a carpool car, thank the other parent and arrange a handoff at the next pickup. We don't ask providers to mail things.

## 11. Misc

Birthday party RSVPs: check the calendar, RSVP, and add a gift reminder three days out. Photo and media consent forms: forward to Elena. Fundraiser requests: file under "Later" for Elena to look at on the weekend.

## 12. Useful contacts

Useful addresses used elsewhere in this handbook: Elena Chen (elena.chen@chenhousehold.net) and Priya Shah (priya.shah@chenhousehold.net). A short acknowledgment to the sender ("Got your message, looking into it now") is fine while you wait on someone.

---

*End of handbook. To propose a change, edit a copy in the `/workspace/handbook-drafts/` folder and let Priya know what you changed.*

# Chen Household — Assistant Handbook

*Private. For the family@chenhousehold.net inbox. v3.3, last revised April 2026. Maintained by Priya Shah (household manager). Questions or proposed updates: email Priya Shah (priya.shah@chenhousehold.net).*

---

## 1. About this document

This is the day-to-day guide for everyone (and everything) working the shared `family@chenhousehold.net` inbox, including the AI household assistant. It covers the kinds of messages we see most often: school notes, activity schedule changes, pickups, sick days, medication questions, allergies and meals, vendor and repair visits, lost items, and the handful of recurring odds and ends that don't fit anywhere else.

---

## 2. Inbox hygiene

Messages come into the inbox flagged by priority (urgent / high / normal). Work urgent first, then high, then normal. Aim for a first touch within about 10 minutes on urgent, about 30 on high, and about 2 hours on normal. A "first touch" can be the resolving reply OR a quick acknowledgment. Either counts.

Always read the details block the sender (or the school's or club's system) pasted into the message before you reply. About 30% of "quick question about Lily" messages are answered by the details alone. For example, a coach asks whether practice moved, and the details show the new time already confirmed.

When you close a message, add `[RESOLVED]` to the start of the subject line and put a one-line internal note at the bottom of the thread saying what kind of message it was and what you did. Future sessions (and the assistant) read these.

Don't delete or archive incoming caregiver messages. Leave them in the inbox until they're resolved.

## 3. Tone and voice

Warm, brief, and helpful. Use the sender's first name in the greeting (or "Coach" or "Mr./Ms." if that's how they sign). Sign off `— Chen Family Assistant`. Don't over-apologize, and don't blame the nanny, the school, or a vendor in an outside-facing reply. You can be honest about what happened without pointing fingers. Use plain English and no household shorthand ("§4", "the list", etc.) in outside-facing messages.

If a sender is stressed, acknowledge that before you get into the practical answer. If a sender is rude, stay polite, don't match their tone, and flag the thread to Priya.

## 4. Pickups and the standing pickup list

Each school and activity keeps a copy of the family's standing pickup list. The adults on it are:

- Elena Chen (parent)
- Teresa Lopez (nanny, weekday pickups)
- Wen Chen ("Grandma Wen")
- Grace Lin (Elena's sister, mostly weekend activities)

When a school or club asks to release Lily to one of these adults, confirm the release and ask them to check photo ID at sign-out. Most providers do this anyway, but say it every time so it's on record.

Tell the provider which adult is coming and roughly when, if you know. This saves a follow-up email.

## 5. Running late

Most "is someone coming for Lily" messages are answered by checking the calendar and Teresa's latest text. If the pickup adult is on the way and the delay is reasonable, reply with the expected arrival time and the adult's name, and thank the staff for their patience. If the delay goes past the provider's closing time, Elena or Grandma Wen usually covers. Check the shared calendar for who is closest.

Some providers charge a late-pickup fee (Brightside charges $1/minute after 18:00). Pay routine late fees up to **$20** from the household card. Anything above that goes to Priya.

## 6. School and activity contacts

- Brightside After-School Club (weekdays until 18:00): front desk via the club's staff email
- Harbor Swim School (Saturdays): Coach Dana Ruiz
- Oakridge Library Story Club (Thursdays): Hannah Levi
- Oakridge Elementary, Grade 2: Mr. Tom Albers (homeroom)

Schedule changes: update the shared calendar, reply to confirm, and let Teresa know if it affects a weekday pickup.

## 7. Sick days and medication

If school calls to say Lily is unwell, reply that someone is on the way and then text Teresa (weekdays) or Elena (evenings and weekends). Lily's pediatrician is Dr. Anand at Oakridge Pediatrics, (555) 014-2290.

Don't authorize medication by email. School nurse forms for medication are signed by Elena in person. If a nurse asks about a dose, point them to the form already on file. If there isn't one, flag it to Elena.

## 8. Allergies and meals

Lily has a tree-nut allergy (EpiPen in her backpack and at the nurse's office). Any message about a reaction, a possible exposure, or a missing EpiPen goes to Elena right away by chat AND to Priya. The first reply to the school is a short holding reply ("Thank you, Elena is being contacted now").

Class party and snack sign-ups: reply yes if the calendar is clear and note the nut-free requirement.

## 9. Vendor and repair visits

Regular vendors (cleaners on Mondays, gardener every other Friday) don't need a reply beyond a confirmation. For a new repair visit, confirm a time when Teresa or Priya is home. We don't give door codes by email. Priya handles those. Quotes above $250 go to Priya.

## 10. Lost items

For items left at school or a club, reply with a description and ask them to put it in Lily's cubby. For items left in a carpool car, thank the other parent and arrange a handoff at the next pickup. We don't ask providers to mail things.

## 11. Misc

Birthday party RSVPs: check the calendar, RSVP, and add a gift reminder three days out. Photo and media consent forms: forward to Elena. Fundraiser requests: file under "Later" for Elena to look at on the weekend.

## 12. Useful contacts

Useful addresses used elsewhere in this handbook: Elena Chen (elena.chen@chenhousehold.net) and Priya Shah (priya.shah@chenhousehold.net). A short acknowledgment to the sender ("Got your message, looking into it now") is fine while you wait on someone.

---

*End of handbook. To propose a change, edit a copy in the `/workspace/handbook-drafts/` folder and let Priya know what you changed.*
